deckTitle: The Architecture of Grace — Book 2: The Framework — Grades 3-5 Upper Elementary Edition — Scenario Card Deck
sourceNote: SOURCE PDF IS A FREE PREVIEW: it contains only Unit 1, Lessons 1–2 (cards 1-A through 1-D). The full deck is 28 lessons / 56 cards. Remaining units and lesson titles below come from the deck's Table of Contents only; their cards are not present in the source.
howToUse: Each page contains two scenario cards for a single lesson. The page is designed to be printed and cut along the marked cut lines.
Cards are color-coded by unit: Navy = Unit 1, Teal = Unit 2, Purple = Unit 3, Green = Unit 4.
Laminating the cards allows reuse across multiple class periods and school years.
Each card contains: The Situation (read aloud or displayed), Discussion Questions (guide the conversation), and where relevant, a Teacher Note (italicized—not read to students).
Risk-flagged lessons (★ Elevated, ★★ Highest Risk) are marked on the lesson header. See the Teacher Master Document for full Safety Check protocols before delivering these lessons.
Scenario cards are also embedded in their lessons in the Teacher Master Document for reference during delivery.

cards.title: Who Am I?
cards.situation: Marcus shared on his identity web that he loves drawing comics. A classmate said, "That's babyish." Marcus feels embarrassed and wishes he had said something else.
questions: Is Marcus's love of comics part of who he truly is?
Why does a classmate's comment make him want to hide it?
What is the difference between something being part of your identity and something being "cool" according to others?
What would you say to Marcus to help him hold his identity with confidence?

cards.title: Who Am I?
cards.situation: Amara is filling out her strengths inventory and cannot think of a single thing to write. She keeps crossing things out. "I'm not really good at anything," she tells her partner. Her partner looks surprised.
questions: Why might Amara struggle to name her own strengths, even though others can see them?
What is the difference between a strength you were born with and one you developed through effort?
If you were Amara's partner, what specific strength might you have already noticed about her in just this one class?

cards.title: Emotions Are Information
cards.situation: During a math test, Jayla's mind goes blank even though she studied. She feels a wave of panic. After the test: "I hate when that happens—my feelings always ruin everything."
questions: What message was Jayla's panic actually trying to send her?
Is Jayla's emotion the problem—or is it a messenger pointing at a different problem?
If Jayla could name the emotion precisely, how might that help her next time?

cards.title: Emotions Are Information
cards.situation: Deon gets in the car after school and says "Fine" when asked about his day—but he actually felt lonely, left out, and invisible. He didn't have words for it.
questions: What emotions was Deon actually feeling? Can you name them more precisely than "fine"?
What message were those emotions trying to carry?
Why might it be hard to share emotions, even when we do have words for them?
